title: Sanding dust and silica exposure controls
audience: Plasterers and handyman workers who sand plaster, joint compound or older coatings
learningOutcomes: Identify the dust that sanding plaster produces and the exposure route it creates.
Apply wet methods, extraction and suitable respiratory protection to control dust.
Stop sanding older or unknown material until its composition is assessed.

instruction.heading: Where the dust comes from
instruction.body: Sanding plaster, joint compound and some sand-based products produces fine dust. Some plaster and sand products contain crystalline silica, and inhaling fine silica dust is a serious health risk. Dust can also come from older coatings and from materials in older buildings that may contain asbestos. The control method depends on what the material is, and an unknown material is treated as hazardous until it is identified or assessed. Check the product safety data sheet for the material before sanding. The workplace exposure standard for respirable crystalline silica is 0.05 mg/m3 as an 8-hour time-weighted average, half the earlier 0.1 mg/m3 figure (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown; Safe Work Australia research page, no date shown).

instruction.heading: Control the dust at source
instruction.body: Use wet methods where the product allows them, because wet material produces much less airborne dust. Where dry sanding is used, use a power sander connected to extraction with a suitable filter, and keep the work area ventilated. Keep occupants and children away, close doors, and cover vents and ducts. Clean up with damp methods and an extraction unit suited to fine dust, and do not dry sweep. Wear respiratory protection suited to the dust and fitted correctly, and change or clean it as the manufacturer directs.

procedure: Check the safety data sheet for the material and identify any silica or other hazardous content.
Stop and refer if the material is older or unknown until its composition is confirmed.
Use wet methods where the product allows them.
Where dry sanding is used, connect the sander to extraction and keep the area ventilated.
Keep occupants and children away, and seal the area from the rest of the building.
Clean up with damp methods or an extraction unit, and do not dry sweep; record the controls used.

workedExamples.situation: A worker is asked to dry sand a patch of old wall finish in a 1960s flat, and the worker is not sure what the finish contains.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the dry sanding go ahead?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The material is older and its composition is unknown, so it may contain asbestos or silica. Stop, keep people away, and refer for assessment before any sanding. Use wet methods only after the composition is confirmed and the controls are set.

equipmentAndPpe: Respiratory protection suited to the dust, fitted correctly
Extraction-connected sander with a suitable filter
Damp cloths and a HEPA-filtered vacuum where suitable

commonErrors.error: Dry sanding plaster without extraction or respiratory protection.
commonErrors.prevention: Use wet methods, or extraction with suitable respiratory protection.

commonErrors.error: Sanding an older or unknown finish without assessment.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop and refer until the composition is confirmed.

commonErrors.error: Dry sweeping the dust after the job.
commonErrors.prevention: Use damp methods or an extraction unit suited to fine dust.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Asbestos. Victoria: an employer, or a person working for themselves, can remove non-friable asbestos without a licence where the area of asbestos-containing material to be removed does not exceed 10 square metres in total, and the total time asbestos removal work is performed in any period of seven days does not exceed one hour, which is cumulative across all employees; friable asbestos has no such allowance (Asbestos Victoria page, which shows an 'Updated' label and no date). Removal above either limit needs a licence. New South Wales: a class B licence is not needed for less than 10 m2 of non-friable material (Service NSW page, last published 24 July 2025). Queensland: non-friable work of 10 m2 at most needs no licence, but friable material of any quantity needs a class A licence (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown).

Silica dust: the workplace exposure standard is 0.05 mg/m3 as an 8-hour time-weighted average (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown; Safe Work Australia research page, no date shown, which says to confirm the figure with the state or territory regulator). This is an exposure limit, not a licence, and this lesson does not grant any licence.
Completing this lesson does not give an asbestos removal licence or any authority to remove older materials.

qualityStandard: The material's composition is known or assessed before any sanding.
Dust is controlled at source with wet methods or extraction, and suitable respiratory protection is worn.
Clean-up is done with damp methods or extraction, not dry sweeping.
documentationEvidence: Safety data sheet check record for the material
Dust control record with method and protection used
Referral note for older or unknown material
summary: Identify the material and its hazard before sanding.
Control dust at source with wet methods or extraction and suitable protection.
Stop and refer older or unknown material.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker is asked to dry sand an old wall finish of unknown composition. What is correct?
options: Dry sand it quickly, since the finish is only a thin paint layer
Sand it wet without checking what the finish is made of
Sand it and dry sweep the dust into a bin afterwards to finish
Stop, keep people away, and refer for assessment before sanding

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the preferred way to reduce airborne dust when sanding plaster?
options: Use wet methods where the product allows, or extraction with suitable respiratory protection
Open the windows and carry on, since the air will clear the dust out of the room quickly
Dry sweep after each wall, since the broom clears the dust quickly and easily from the floor
Use a fan to blow the dust outside through the window of the room while you work on the wall

knowledgeChecks.question: What health risk does the lesson link to inhaling fine silica dust?
options: No risk when the room is ventilated
